label: L19
title: Prescriptive Neural Networks with Explainability
brief: The optimal prescription problem asks which treatment to give each individual, from observational data, to minimize (or maximize) an outcome; treatments can be binary, single or multiple continuous, or multiple discrete. Prescriptive Neural Networks (PNNs) extend Optimal Policy Trees to multimodal data in four steps: extract embeddings per modality, estimate counterfactual outcomes for every treatment (direct or doubly-robust method) into a rewards matrix $\Gamma$, train a feedforward network whose softmax output assigns treatment probabilities by minimizing the expected estimated outcome, and explain the result. Explanations come from a Mirrored OCT (an Optimal Classification Tree trained to reproduce the PNN's prescriptions) for tabular data, or from an LLM in the xHAIM style for multimodal data. Across TAVR valve choice, liver and spleen injury, diabetes dosing, strawberry pricing and REBOA, PNNs and Mirrored OCTs match or beat regress-and-compare, causal forests and Optimal Policy Trees, and multimodal data raise the TAVR improvement from about 5-8% to about 42-43%. The TAVR vs SAVR case study adds confounding by surgical risk, handled with prognostic matching within STS-risk buckets, and a policy chosen by trading sensitivity against specificity.
kp: Optimal prescription problem: for observation $x_i$, choose treatment $t \in T$ to minimize outcome $y_i$; treatments may be single binary, single continuous, multiple continuous or multiple discrete.
Existing methods: regress-and-compare, causal forests, causal deep learning, Optimal Policy Trees and Optimal Prescriptive Trees.
Why PNNs: they use multimodal data, neural nets have more modeling power than trees, and they scale better with many treatments.
PNN pipeline: (1) embedding extraction, (2) counterfactual estimation, (3) PNN training with a prescriptive loss, (4) explainability (Mirrored OCT for tabular, LLMs for multimodal).
Counterfactuals: the direct method fits one regression per treatment (suffers treatment assignment bias); doubly-robust adds a propensity classifier and re-weights the direct estimates.
Rewards matrix $\Gamma$: $\Gamma_{i,t}$ is the estimated outcome of giving treatment $t$ to patient $i$.

PNN loss: $\min \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \sum_{t=1}^{N_t} \mathbb{P}(\tau(x_i)=t)\,\Gamma_{i,t}$, the softmax relaxation of the OPT objective with indicators $\mathbb{1}\{\tau(x_i)=t\}$, which makes it differentiable.
Mirrored OCT: an OCT trained on the original features with the PNN's prescriptions as target classes, recovering interpretability with little loss in performance.
Evaluation: many random 50/50 train/test splits; report average relative improvement of the outcome on the test set.

TAVR vs SAVR: assignment is confounded by STS surgical risk, so prognostic matching is done within STS-risk buckets; the chosen policy balances estimated mortality improvement against how many treatments change (sensitivity vs specificity).

topics.x: Given observational data $\{x_i\}$ (demographics, prescriptions, notes, images, time series) and outcomes $\{y_i\}$, pick for each individual the treatment that optimizes the outcome. Treatments range from a single binary choice to multiple continuous doses, and existing solutions include regress-and-compare, causal forests and policy or prescriptive trees.

Each modality is turned into features: tabular data are normalized, text and images go through pretrained models (BERT, Clinical Longformer, DenseNet). Since each patient's outcome is observed under only one treatment, the missing counterfactual outcomes are estimated (direct or doubly-robust) to fill the rewards matrix $\Gamma$.

A feedforward network with ReLU hidden layers and a softmax output gives $\mathbb{P}(\tau(x_i)=t)$ for each treatment. Training minimizes the probability-weighted estimated outcome, a differentiable version of the Optimal Policy Tree objective that uses hard indicators.

Neural networks are black boxes. For tabular data a Mirrored OCT is trained on the features with the PNN's prescriptions as labels; for multimodal data the xHAIM framework is extended so an LLM combines notes, imaging reports, tabular data, the PNN prescription and medical knowledge into a grounded explanation.

Models are compared over many random 50/50 splits by the average relative improvement of the test-set outcome. On TAVR valve choice, liver injury, diabetes, strawberry pricing, spleen injuries and REBOA, PNNs and Mirrored OCTs perform better than or comparably to the baselines; regress-and-compare and causal forests even turn negative on REBOA.

The task is to choose TAVR (minimally invasive) or SAVR (open-heart surgery) to minimize long-term mortality using demographics, comorbidities, notes and CT scans across Hartford and St. Vincent's cohorts. Because TAVR is far more common in high-STS-risk patients, prognostic matching within risk buckets balances the cohort, and the final policy trades sensitivity (changing treatment for adverse outcomes) against specificity (keeping it for favorable ones).

cards.b: From observational data $\{x_i\}$ with outcomes $\{y_i\}$, for a given observation $x_i$ find the treatment $t \in T$ that minimizes (or maximizes) the outcome $y_i$.
cards.x: Only one treatment's outcome is ever observed per patient; the rest must be estimated.

cards.f: Four kinds of treatment sets in prescription problems.
cards.b: Single discrete (binary), single continuous, multiple continuous, multiple discrete.
cards.x: E.g. TAVR valve = binary, strawberry price = single continuous, diabetes drug doses = multiple continuous, spleen treatment = multiple discrete.

cards.f: Three reasons to use Prescriptive Neural Networks rather than trees.
cards.b: (1) They can leverage multimodal data. (2) Neural networks are empirically shown to have more modeling power than trees. (3) They scale better with a large number of treatments.
cards.x: Interpretability is NOT a PNN advantage; that is why a Mirrored OCT or LLM is added.

cards.f: The four steps of the PNN framework.
cards.b: (1) Embedding extraction. (2) Counterfactual estimation. (3) Train a feedforward network with a prescriptive objective. (4) Explainability: Mirrored OCT for tabular data, LLMs for multimodal data.
cards.x: Steps 2 and 3 mirror the Optimal Policy Tree pipeline; steps 1 and 4 handle multimodality.

cards.f: How is each data type prepared in the embedding step?
cards.b: Structured/tabular data: appropriate processing such as normalization. Language: embeddings from pretrained models (e.g. BERT, Clinical Longformer). Images: embeddings from pretrained models (e.g. DenseNet).
cards.x: Embeddings become the input vector $x$ of the PNN.

cards.f: What is a counterfactual in the prescription setting?
cards.b: The unknown outcome for an observation under a treatment it did not receive (the '?' cells of the patient x treatment table).
cards.x: Each row of the table has exactly one observed entry.

cards.f: Direct method vs doubly-robust counterfactual estimation.
cards.b: Direct: one regression model per treatment type, which suffers from treatment assignment bias. Doubly-robust: (a) a classification model estimates propensity scores (treatment assignment probabilities); (b) the propensity scores re-weight the direct-method estimates.
cards.x: The propensity correction targets the bias from who historically got which treatment.

cards.b: The completed patient x treatment table: $\Gamma_{i,t}$ is the estimated outcome of applying treatment $t$ to patient $i$.
cards.x: The PNN never sees raw outcomes directly; it optimizes against $\Gamma$.

cards.b: $\min \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{t=1}^{N_t} \mathbb{P}(\tau(x_i)=t)\,\Gamma_{i,t}$, where $\mathbb{P}(\tau(x_i)=t)$ is the network's softmax output for treatment $t$.
cards.x: It is the expected estimated outcome under the network's randomized prescription.

cards.f: How does the Optimal Policy Tree objective differ from the PNN loss?
cards.b: OPT uses hard indicators $\mathbb{1}\{\tau(x_i)=t\}$ (one treatment per patient); the PNN replaces them with softmax probabilities $\mathbb{P}(\tau(x_i)=t)$, giving a differentiable loss.
cards.x: Same objective idea, relaxed so gradient-based training works.

cards.b: Input $x$; hidden layers $y^{(l)} = W^{(l)} z^{(l-1)} + b^{(l)}$ with $z^{(l)} = \mathrm{ReLU}(y^{(l)})$; output layer with $z = \mathrm{Softmax}(y)$, one output per treatment: $\sigma_t(z) = \exp(z_t)/\sum_{t'} \exp(z_{t'})$.
cards.x: Architecturally it is a multiclass classifier; only the loss is prescriptive.

cards.b: An Optimal Classification Tree trained on the original data's features with the PNN's prescriptions as the target classes.
cards.x: It mirrors the PNN's decisions, not the observed treatments or outcomes.

cards.f: How are PNN prescriptions explained for multimodal data?
cards.b: By extending xHAIM: an LLM combines the notes, imaging report, tabular data, the PNN prescription and medical knowledge into grounded, factual explanations (e.g. why SAVR is recommended for a 74-year-old with a heavily calcified valve).
cards.x: A tree on embeddings would not be readable, so text explanations replace it.

cards.f: How are prescriptive models evaluated in the experiments?
cards.b: Split into many randomized 50% train / 50% test sets, train each model class on each split, and report the average relative improvement of the outcome on the test set.
cards.x: Improvement is measured against estimated counterfactuals, so the estimator's quality matters.

cards.f: Why is prognostic matching used in the TAVR vs SAVR study, and how?
cards.b: Treatment assignment is strongly confounded: TAVR is much more common among high-STS-risk patients. Within each STS-risk bucket, each minority-treatment patient is matched to the closest majority-treatment patient on STS risk and clinical covariates, giving a more balanced cohort and more reliable treatment-effect estimates.
cards.x: Matching inside risk buckets compares like with like.

cards.f: Define sensitivity and specificity for a prescription policy (TAVR vs SAVR).
cards.b: Sensitivity $= |\{i: y_i=1, \hat t_i \ne t_i\}| / |\{i: y_i=1\}|$: change treatment among patients with adverse outcomes. Specificity $= |\{i: y_i=0, \hat t_i = t_i\}| / |\{i: y_i=0\}|$: keep treatment among patients with favorable outcomes.
cards.x: Not the classifier definitions: here 'positive' means changing the treatment of a patient who did badly.

quiz.q: What does the optimal prescription problem ask?
o: Which treatment to give each individual to optimize a specific outcome
Which patients will have the worst outcome
How to estimate the average treatment effect over a population
Which features best predict the observed treatment
quiz.e: It is a per-individual decision: the treatment that minimizes (or maximizes) that person's outcome. Predicting outcomes or the population average effect are inputs at best, not the decision itself.

quiz.q: Which of these is NOT given in the lecture as a reason to use Prescriptive Neural Networks?
o: Neural networks are directly interpretable
They can leverage multimodal data
Neural networks have shown more modeling power than trees
They scale better with a large number of treatments
quiz.e: Networks are black boxes; interpretability has to be added afterwards with a Mirrored OCT or an LLM. The other three are the three listed motivations.

quiz.q: In the direct method of counterfactual estimation, what is trained?
o: One regression model for each treatment type
One classifier that predicts which treatment was given
A single regression on all patients ignoring treatment
An Optimal Classification Tree on the prescriptions
quiz.e: The direct method fits a separate outcome regression per treatment. A treatment classifier is the propensity model used by the doubly-robust method.

quiz.q: Why does the doubly-robust method add a propensity-score model to the direct method?
o: The direct method suffers from treatment assignment bias, which re-weighting by propensity scores corrects
The direct method cannot handle continuous outcomes
Propensity scores replace the need for outcome regressions entirely
It makes the PNN loss differentiable
quiz.e: Patients were not assigned treatments at random, so per-treatment regressions are biased; propensity scores re-weight those estimates. The doubly-robust method still uses the outcome regressions, it does not replace them.

quiz.q: In the rewards matrix, what is $\Gamma_{i,t}$?
o: The estimated outcome of applying treatment $t$ to patient $i$
The probability that patient $i$ received treatment $t$
The PNN's probability of prescribing $t$ to patient $i$
The observed outcome of patient $i$
quiz.e: $\Gamma$ is the completed counterfactual table of estimated outcomes. Assignment probabilities are propensity scores; prescription probabilities are the PNN's softmax outputs.

quiz.q: In the lecture example, patient 1 has $\Gamma_{1,\cdot} = (0.82, 0.76, 0.78)$ and PNN output $(0.2, 0.45, 0.35)$. What is patient 1's term in the PNN objective (before dividing by $N$)?
quiz.e: $0.2(0.82) + 0.45(0.76) + 0.35(0.78) = 0.164 + 0.342 + 0.273 = 0.779$. 0.760 is the hard OPT term for the best treatment; 0.787 is the unweighted row mean.

quiz.q: In the lecture example, the Optimal Policy Tree prescribes $t_2, t_2, t_3, t_2$ to patients 1-4 with rows $(0.82,0.76,0.78)$, $(0.45,0.36,0.40)$, $(0.38,0.39,0.30)$, $(0.53,0.44,0.45)$. What is its objective (sum over patients, no $1/N$)?
quiz.e: $0.76 + 0.36 + 0.30 + 0.44 = 1.86$. 1.985 is the PNN's soft objective and 2.19 sums the row maxima.

quiz.q: Using the same example, PNN outputs for patients 1-4 are $(0.2,0.45,0.35)$, $(0.1,0.6,0.3)$, $(0.45,0.4,0.15)$, $(0.1,0.5,0.4)$. What is the PNN objective (sum, no $1/N$), and how does it compare with the OPT's 1.86?
o: About 1.985, higher than the OPT's because probability mass sits on worse treatments
About 1.985, lower than the OPT's because soft assignments hedge
About 1.86, equal to the OPT's
About 1.79, lower than the OPT's
quiz.e: Patient terms: 0.779, 0.381, 0.372, 0.453, summing to 1.985. Since we minimize, 1.985 > 1.86 is worse: some probability is placed on treatments with higher estimated outcomes (e.g. patient 3 puts 0.45 on $t_1$).

quiz.q: Why does the PNN loss use softmax probabilities $\mathbb{P}(\tau(x_i)=t)$ instead of the indicator $\mathbb{1}\{\tau(x_i)=t\}$ used by Optimal Policy Trees?
o: To make the loss differentiable so the network can be trained by gradient methods
To estimate counterfactual outcomes
To guarantee the prescription is interpretable
To correct treatment assignment bias
quiz.e: The goal is a differentiable loss representing the estimated average outcome. Counterfactuals and bias correction happen in step 2, before the PNN.

quiz.q: What activations does the PNN use?
o: ReLU in hidden layers, softmax at the output
Sigmoid in hidden layers, linear output
Softmax in every layer
ReLU everywhere, including the output
quiz.e: Hidden layers are ReLU; the output layer is a softmax over treatments so it yields assignment probabilities. A ReLU output would not give probabilities that sum to one.

quiz.q: How is a Mirrored OCT trained?
o: On the original features, with the PNN's prescriptions as target classes
On the original features, with the observed treatments as targets
On the counterfactual matrix $\Gamma$ as a regression target
On the PNN's hidden-layer embeddings
quiz.e: It mirrors the PNN: the labels are what the PNN prescribes. Using observed treatments would imitate past practice, not the optimized policy.

quiz.q: For multimodal data, how does the PNN framework provide explanations?
o: An LLM, extending xHAIM, combines the patient's data, the PNN prescription and medical knowledge
A Mirrored OCT trained on the image embeddings
Saliency maps over the CT scans
Feature importances from a causal forest
quiz.e: For multimodal data the explainability step uses LLMs that produce grounded, factual explanations. The Mirrored OCT is the tabular-data route.

quiz.q: How are prescriptive models evaluated in the lecture's experiments?
o: Average relative improvement of the outcome on the test set over many random 50/50 splits
Classification accuracy of the prescribed vs observed treatment
Training loss on a single 80/20 split
AUC of the counterfactual estimator
quiz.e: The metric is outcome improvement, averaged over many randomized 50% train/50% test splits. Agreement with the observed treatment is not the goal; the goal is better outcomes.

quiz.q: In the TAVR valve-selection experiment (minimize pacemaker implantation), which setting gave the largest improvement, about 42-43%?
o: Multimodal data for both the counterfactual estimator and the model
Tabular data for both the estimator and the model
A multimodal estimator with a tabular model only
Regress-and-compare with tabular data
quiz.e: Multimodal/multimodal gives 42.89% (PNN) and 41.66% (Mirrored OCT). All-tabular gives only 5.05% and 7.67%, so using the reports and scans matters a lot.

quiz.q: In the REBOA experiment, regress-and-compare and causal forests show improvements of about -19%. What does a negative value mean?
o: Following their prescriptions is estimated to worsen mortality relative to the observed treatments
They beat the PNN by 19%
Their training failed to converge
They prescribed REBOA to 19% fewer patients
quiz.e: Improvement is the relative change in the outcome; negative means the policy does worse than current practice. OPT, PNN and Mirrored OCT reach about +17-18%.

quiz.q: The spleen-injury study chooses among splenectomy, angioembolization and observation. What type of treatment is this?
o: Multiple discrete
Single binary
Single continuous
Multiple continuous
quiz.e: Three distinct, non-numeric options make it multiple discrete. Diabetes dosing is the multiple-continuous example.

quiz.q: A TAVR/SAVR policy is evaluated on 40 patients with adverse outcomes ($y=1$) and 160 with favorable ones ($y=0$). It changes the treatment of 30 of the 40 and keeps the treatment of 120 of the 160. What are its sensitivity and specificity?
o: Sensitivity 0.75, specificity 0.75
Sensitivity 0.25, specificity 0.75
Sensitivity 0.75, specificity 0.25
Sensitivity 0.15, specificity 0.60
quiz.e: Sensitivity = changed among $y=1$ = 30/40 = 0.75. Specificity = kept among $y=0$ = 120/160 = 0.75. Mixing up 'changed' and 'kept' gives the 0.25 answers.

quiz.q: Why does the TAVR vs SAVR study match patients within STS-risk buckets?
o: TAVR is much more common among high-risk patients, so treatment is confounded; matching balances the groups
STS risk is the outcome to be minimized
Matching increases the sample size of the training set
The PNN cannot take STS risk as an input
quiz.e: Higher-risk patients mostly got TAVR, so raw comparisons mix treatment effect with risk. Matching each minority-group patient to the closest majority-group patient on risk and covariates makes effect estimates more reliable. Matching does not add data.

written.q: A hospital has observational data on patients who received one of three treatments, with tabular records, clinical notes and images, and wants a policy minimizing 1-year mortality. (a) Describe the four steps of the PNN framework for this problem. (b) Write the PNN loss and explain how it relates to the Optimal Policy Tree objective. (c) How would you explain the policy to clinicians?
written.m: (a) Step 1, embeddings: normalize tabular features; embed notes with a pretrained language model (e.g. BERT/Clinical Longformer) and images with a pretrained vision model (e.g. DenseNet); concatenate into $x_i$. Step 2, counterfactuals: each patient has one observed outcome; estimate the others with the direct method (one regression per treatment) or, to reduce treatment assignment bias, doubly-robust (propensity classifier re-weighting the direct estimates); this gives $\Gamma_{i,t}$. Step 3, PNN: a feedforward net with ReLU hidden layers and a 3-way softmax output $\mathbb{P}(\tau(x_i)=t)$. Step 4, explainability. (b) $\min \frac1N\sum_i\sum_t \mathbb{P}(\tau(x_i)=t)\Gamma_{i,t}$. OPT minimizes $\frac1N\sum_i\sum_t \mathbb{1}\{\tau(x_i)=t\}\Gamma_{i,t}$ with a tree; the PNN replaces the indicator with softmax probabilities so the loss is differentiable and can be trained by gradient methods on multimodal inputs. The prescription is the treatment with the highest probability. (c) Because the inputs are multimodal, use the LLM route (xHAIM extension): combine the patient's notes, imaging report, tabular data, the PNN prescription and medical knowledge into a grounded explanation. For a tabular-only version, fit a Mirrored OCT on the features with the PNN prescriptions as labels and show the tree. Evaluate with many random 50/50 splits and average relative improvement in mortality.
k: Embeddings per modality with pretrained models
Counterfactual estimation: direct vs doubly-robust, propensity scores, rewards matrix
Correct PNN loss with softmax probabilities
Relation to OPT: indicator relaxed to probability, differentiable
Explainability: LLM for multimodal, Mirrored OCT for tabular
Evaluation by relative improvement over random splits

written.q: In the TAVR vs SAVR study, (a) explain why naive counterfactual estimation would be biased and how prognostic matching addresses it; (b) define sensitivity and specificity for a prescription policy and explain why the chosen policy balances them against estimated mortality improvement.
written.m: (a) Treatment assignment is strongly confounded: TAVR is much more common among patients with higher STS surgical risk, so outcomes under TAVR come mostly from sicker patients. Regressions fit per treatment would mix the effect of the procedure with the effect of risk. Prognostic matching groups patients into STS-risk buckets and, within each bucket, matches each patient in the minority treatment group to the closest patient in the majority group on STS risk and clinical covariates. The matched cohort is more balanced and comparable across treatments, which makes the downstream treatment-effect estimates more reliable. (b) Sensitivity = fraction of patients with adverse outcomes ($y=1$) whose treatment the policy changes ($\hat t_i \ne t_i$); specificity = fraction of patients with favorable outcomes ($y=0$) whose treatment it keeps. A policy that changes many treatments may show large estimated mortality gains but contradicts practice for patients who did well (low specificity); a cautious one keeps treatments but helps few who did badly (low sensitivity). The selected policy balances estimated mortality improvement against the number of treatment changes, and different modalities give different trade-offs.
k: Confounding by STS risk: TAVR concentrated in high-risk patients
Matching within STS buckets on risk and covariates
Result: balanced, comparable cohort, more reliable effect estimates
Trade-off between improvement and treatment changes
